title: Stable and Near-Reversible Diffusion ODE Solvers for Image Editing

paper.title: Stable and Near-Reversible Diffusion ODE Solvers for Image Editing
paper.abstract: Abstract The inversion of diffusion models plays a central role in image editing. Algebraically reversible ODE solvers provide an appealing approach to diffusion inversion for text-guided image editing, by eliminating the inversion error inherent in DDIM-based editing pipelines. However, empirical results indicate that reversibility alone is insufficient. As edits require larger semantic or visual changes, reversible diffusion solvers often exhibit instabilities and suffer sharp drops in output quality. In this paper, we show that the trade-off between exact reversibility and numerical stability manifests empirically as a trade-off between background preservation and prompt alignment in image editing. We then investigate the use of near-reversible Runge–Kutta methods as a more stable alternative to exactly reversible diffusion schemes. When combined with a vector-field smoothing strategy, the resulting approach improves edit fidelity, remains stable under large edits, and largely retains the background-preservation benefits of reversible solvers.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion probabilistic models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2020b ) have become a standard tool for text-guided image editing ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Nichol et al., 2021 ) . A common approach is inversion-based editing —given a real image, the probability-flow ODE ( Song et al., 2020b ) is integrated backwards in time to a latent noise state conditional on a source prompt, after which the forward ODE is integrated under a new target prompt to obtain an edited image ( Song et al., 2020a ; Mokady et al., 2023 ; Ju et al., 2023 ) . (a) Small Edits (b) Large Edits Figure 1 : Qualitative comparison of (near) reversible solvers on image editing tasks. ( 1(a) ) Standard PIE-Bench editing tasks ( Section 5.2 ). Here, we use Smooth Diffusion for BELM, EDICT, and EES. ( 1(b) ) PIE-Bench images with large prompt deviations ( Section 5.3 ) and greyscale conversion ( Section E.3 ). Here, we use Smooth Diffusion for all methods. See extended grids in Figures 17 , 15 , 18 and 9 . In this setting, the choice of numerical solver is vital, since errors resulting from inexact inversion compound through the editing process, especially under classifier-free guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ) . For instance, classical DDIM inversion incurs a systematic trajectory mismatch, since the reverse update is not the algebraic inverse of the forward update. A long line of work aims to reduce the resulting diffusion inversion error ( Han et al., 2023 ; Miyake et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2024 ) . Recently, algebraically reversible (or simply reversible ) ODE solvers such as EDICT ( Wallace et al., 2023 ) , BDIA ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , BELM ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , and Rex ( Blasingame and Liu, 2026 ) have been proposed as an alternative to DDIM inversion, yielding improved reconstructions and background preservation in editing pipelines. However, our empirical evidence suggests that reversibility alone is not enough. On standard editing tasks, reversible solvers exhibit a clear trade-off between background preservation and prompt alignment. This becomes particularly apparent when the editing trajectory departs substantially from the inversion trajectory, in which case many reversible solvers suffer sharp drops in edit quality. To benchmark solver performance for image editing, we distinguish two evaluation settings. The first is the widely used small edits setting of the PIE-Bench image editing benchmark introduced by Ju et al. (2023) , where edits are usually local to a subset of the prompt and image (see Section 5.2 ). In addition, we introduce a second large edits regime, where the edited prompt induces a large semantic or visual change, forcing the sampling trajectory away from the original inversion path (see Section 5.3 ). Figure 1 previews the key findings. In Section 4 , we argue that the failure modes of existing reversible schemes, illustrated in Figure 1 , can be attributed to numerical stability. To address these issues, we propose using the recently introduced class of near-reversible Explicit and Effectively Symmetric (EES) Runge–Kutta methods ( Shmelev et al., 2025 ) as diffusion solvers. EES schemes relax exact reversibility, instead enforcing only approximate symmetry up to an acceptably low error tolerance. This relaxation allows them to retain an explicit Runge–Kutta form and benefit from much more favourable stability properties. Since the inversion error depends on the regularity of the underlying trajectory, we additionally combine EES schemes with vector-field smoothing strategies previously proposed for DDIM inversion. Together, this yields a family of solvers that is competitive with exactly reversible solvers on standard editing benchmarks and substantially more stable under challenging edits. In addition to proposing EES solvers, our paper clarifies the broader design space of reversible diffusion solvers for editing. We investigate guidance and smoothing heuristics such as Smooth Diffusion ( Guo et al., 2024 ) , Negative Prompt Inversion ( Miyake et al., 2025 ) , and Proximal Guidance ( Han et al., 2023 ) , which have previously been treated mainly as orthogonal DDIM-based techniques. We show that these methods can also yield substantial gains for reversible solvers, and characterise when they help. We also benchmark Reversible Heun and McCallum–Foster methods, originally introduced outside the diffusion models literature, and run extensive ablations over ODE parametrisations, step schedules, and solver formulations. We summarise our main contributions as follows: 1. We provide a side-by-side evaluation of (near) reversible diffusion solvers for image editing, revealing a trade-off curve between background preservation and prompt alignment. 2. We propose using near-reversible EES Runge–Kutta methods for inversion-based diffusion editing. For small edits , when combined with vector field smoothing, these methods retain much of the background-preservation benefit of exactly reversible solvers while improving edit fidelity. 3. For large edits , we show that EES is the most robust (near) reversible family in our study, maintaining output quality under large trajectory deviations where most exactly reversible solvers degrade substantially.

sections.heading: 2.1 Reversible Solvers
sections.text: In the setting of an autonomous ODE d ​ y t = f ⁡ ( y t ) ​ d ​ t dy_{t}=f(y_{t})dt , a one-step method y n + 1 = y n + h ​ Φ h ​ ( y n ) y_{n+1}=y_{n}+h\Phi_{h}(y_{n}) (1) is said to be symmetric if Φ − h = Φ h − 1 \Phi_{-h}=\Phi_{h}^{-1} . That is, a step of the method Φ \Phi applied to y n + 1 y_{n+1} with a negative step size exactly recovers y n y_{n} . Classical symmetric numerical integration methods, such as those of Runge–Kutta type, have been studied extensively for their favourable long-term behaviour, especially in the context of Hamiltonian systems ( Hairer et al., 2006 ; Feng and Qin, 2010 ; Chartier, 2015 ) . More recently, symmetric methods have proven useful in the training of neural differential equations ( Chen et al., 2018 ) , where the ability to recover the full solution trajectory from the terminal point allows for memory-efficient backpropagation. A major drawback of classical symmetric methods lies in their low efficiency. It is well-known that any symmetric Runge–Kutta scheme is necessarily implicit, and more generally any symmetric parasitism-free general linear method cannot be explicit ( Butcher et al., 2016 ) . This inefficiency makes classical schemes unsuitable for applications in machine learning. To solve this problem, several new algebraically reversible schemes, typically of low-order, were introduced. The asynchronous leapfrog integrator (ALF) ( Zhuang et al., 2021 ) for Neural ODEs overcomes the problem of implicit schemes by tracking an auxiliary state as part of the integration. A similar approach is taken by the Reversible Heun method ( Kidger et al., 2021 ) , where the technique of tracking an auxiliary state is applied to form a reversible version of Heun’s method for SDEs. Whilst both methods prove to be efficient, they are inherently unstable. This instability is a significant bottleneck in certain practical applications ( Shmelev and Salvi, 2025 ; Zhang and Chen, 2021 ) . In ( McCallum and Foster, 2024 ) , a new method was proposed for transforming any existing one-step integration method into one which is reversible. Whilst these methods offer increased stability over the ALF and Reversible Heun solvers, their stability domains are still typically much smaller than those of classical methods. This method was later adapted to the case of diffusion models, where the approach forms the basis for Rex solvers ( Blasingame and Liu, 2026 ) . A potential solution to the issues of stability is offered by Explicit and Effectively Symmetric (EES) Runge–Kutta schemes ( Shmelev et al., 2025 ) . Whilst symmetric Runge–Kutta methods are necessarily implicit, the authors show that it is possible to derive explicit schemes which are almost symmetric, up to a given tolerance level. The resulting schemes are virtually indistinguishable from perfectly symmetric schemes for sufficiently smooth problems and maintain stability domains which are comparable to those of classical schemes such as RK4 and RK5. It was shown in Shmelev and Salvi (2025) that EES schemes produce superior results to Reversible Heun and McCallum-Foster methods when applied to stiff or highly volatile Neural SDEs.

sections.heading: Inversion-driven image editing.
sections.text: A common approach to text-guided image editing with diffusion models is to first invert a real image into the model’s latent noise space and then resample under a new, “edited” prompt ( Song et al., 2020a ; Hertz et al., 2022 ; Mokady et al., 2023 ) . sections.heading: DDIM is not algebraically reversible.
sections.text: It is clear that, since the Euler update rule does not satisfy the symmetry property in Section 2.1 , the DDIM inversion approach is not exact—the forward and backward maps evaluate the network ϵ θ \epsilon_{\theta} at different points x i x_{i} and x i − 1 x_{i-1} . In inversion-driven editing, this mismatch accumulates along the trajectory, leading to low background preservation and a decrease in overall edit quality. Multiple works also observe that the degradation becomes substantially worse under classifier-free guidance, which amplifies per-step errors ( Wallace et al., 2023 ; Hertz et al., 2022 ) .

sections.heading: Mitigating DDIM inversion error.
sections.text: Many works reduce DDIM inversion drift via inference-time or model-level interventions. Smooth Diffusion ( Guo et al., 2024 ) fine-tunes the model to encourage smoother latent geometry, improving inversion and downstream edits. Other methods adjust conditioning during inversion, e.g. null-text inversion (NTI) ( Mokady et al., 2023 ) , negative-prompt inversion (NPI) ( Miyake et al., 2025 ) and proximal guidance ( Han et al., 2023 ) . We summarise the latter two in Section E.1 . Some methods also store and reuse information from the source trajectory to guide editing, e.g. Prompt-to-Prompt ( Hertz et al., 2022 ) , MasaCtrl ( Cao et al., 2023 ) , pix2pic-zero ( Parmar et al., 2023 ) , plug-and-play ( Tumanyan et al., 2023 ) , and Direct Inversion ( Ju et al., 2023 ) . These techniques do not make DDIM algebraically reversible, but often reduce the practical impact of inversion errors.

sections.heading: 3.1 Dependence of EES on Trajectory Regularity
sections.text: We briefly note the dependencies of the error of a near-reversible method on the solution trajectory and its derivatives. Given a numerical method of order n n , it is clear from the definition of order and the Taylor series expansion of the solution that the leading term of the local error takes the form C ​ y t ( n + 1 ) ​ h n + 1 Cy_{t}^{(n+1)}h^{n+1} for some constant C C independent of y y and h h . In a similar fashion, the local “reversibility” error of a reversible solver (that is, the error in recovering the initial condition when the solver is run forwards and then backwards) has a leading term of the form C ​ y t ( m + 1 ) ​ h m + 1 Cy_{t}^{(m+1)}h^{m+1} . As such, regularity of the solution trajectory y t y_{t} and its derivatives plays a significant role in the effectiveness of near-reversible methods such as EES schemes. To mitigate this effect, we apply a number of vector-field smoothing and guidance tricks (see Section 5.1 ).

sections.heading: 3.2 Additional Reversible Solvers
sections.text: For completeness, we also include Reversible Heun ( Kidger et al., 2021 ) and McCallum–Foster ( McCallum and Foster, 2024 ) in our experiments as additional reversible solvers for the diffusion ODE. We use the same probability-flow ODE parametrisation as in Section 3 , but, based on the ablation in Section E.2 , we integrate it directly as a black-box vector field rather than using the rescaled form ( 14 ). We discretise on a uniform t t -grid t 0 , t 1 , … , t N t_{0},t_{1},\ldots,t_{N} and use the corresponding λ t i \lambda_{t_{i}} values. See Appendix C and Appendix D for the exact forms. In Section 5 , we find that although these methods originate from the neural differential equations literature, they are competitive with the other diffusion samplers in our setting.

sections.heading: 4 Stability
sections.text: In this section, we show that EES methods offer significantly stronger stability guarantees than multi-step methods such as BELM, due to their near-symmetric properties and Runge–Kutta type.

sections.heading: 4.1 Multi-Step Methods
sections.text: It is well known that multi-step methods typically possess lower stability than one-step methods. A concrete example of this reduced stability is given by the second Dahlquist barrier ( Dahlquist, 1963 ) , which famously states that no multi-step method of order greater than 2 can be A-stable. The stability of multi-step methods can be difficult to analyse, especially in the case of time-varying coefficients such as the ones used by the BELM sampler ( 9 ). A common proxy for the stability of a linear method is zero-stability , which requires that small perturbations to the initial condition lead to small changes in the numerical solution. An equivalent definition which is aligned closer with the notion of linear-stability of one-step methods is given by the following. Definition 4.1 (Zero-Stability) . Given a linear multistep method, let P P denote the characteristic polynomial which arises from the application of the method to the equation y ′ = 0 y^{\prime}=0 . The method is said to be zero-stable if all roots ζ \zeta of P P satisfy the root condition | ζ | ≤ 1 |\zeta|\leq 1 . As discussed in Wang et al. (2024) , both DDIM and BELM are zero-stable, whilst the zero-stability of the EDICT and BDIA solvers is unclear. Whilst zero-stability is a useful metric for multi-step solvers, the condition is significantly weaker than that of the linear stability of one-step methods. As we will see, the stability guarantees of EES schemes far exceed those of zero-stability.

sections.heading: 4.2 One-Step Methods
sections.text: We begin by defining the more general notion of linear stability . Definition 4.2 . We note that linear stability is a more expressive notion of stability than zero-stability, as the latter corresponds to the case z = 0 z=0 . Theorem 4.3 . Since [ − i , i ] [-i,i] has empty interior in ℂ \mathbb{C} , these methods are nowhere linearly stable . Blasingame and Liu (2026) further show that this is also the case for BDIA and fixed-step O-BELM. sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: In Section 5.1 , we first isolate the role of trajectory regularity. The reconstruction experiments show that the EES reconstruction error grows with vector-field irregularity (i.e. high guidance scale), and that smoothing the vector field substantially reduces this error. This is consistent with the dependence of reversibility error on trajectory regularity discussed in Section 3.1 . In the editing experiments, smoothing also improves background preservation for EES and yields gains for several other solvers. We then evaluate the editing performance of each solver on the small edits PIE-Bench dataset in Section 5.2 . Figure 4 and Table 1 show the trade-off between background preservation and alignment with the intended edit. The optimal solver choice therefore depends on the user’s priorities, and the qualitative examples in Figure 1 make this trade-off visible. Finally, in Section 5.3 , we test the solvers’ robustness under large edits . Table 2 shows that solvers with smaller stability regions visibly degrade in edit quality when the sampling trajectory deviates substantially from the inverted path, whereas EES remains the most reliable of all (near) reversible solvers. Additional results and ablations can be found in Appendix E . Image editing setup. We use Stable Diffusion v1.5 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) as the base model in all experiments. To compare methods under matched compute, we fix a budget of 48 model evaluations per sample and adjust the number of inference steps accordingly: 48 steps for BDIA, BELM, and DDIM; 24 steps for EDICT and Reversible Heun; 16 steps for EES(2,5); and 12 steps for EES(2,7). Rex and McCallum–Foster require twice as many model evaluations as their base solvers, making higher-order or adaptive-step variants too expensive for our 48-evaluation setup. Hence, we choose to benchmark against Rex/McCallum–Foster (Euler) and Rex/McCallum–Foster (Midpoint), using 24 and 12 steps, respectively. We use the standard inversion strength s = 0.8 s=0.8 , as defined by EDICT, for the editing experiments in Section 5.1.2 and Section 5.2 , and s = 1 s=1 in the stability study in Section 5.3 , where stronger edits are required. Following previous work, we fix the editing guidance scale at g = 3.0 g=3.0 . We keep the recommended hyperparameters for EDICT ( p = 0.93 p=0.93 ), BDIA ( γ = 0.96 ) (\gamma=0.96) , and Rex/McCallum–Foster ( ζ = 0.999 \zeta=0.999 ). Editing benchmark and metrics We evaluate on PIE-Bench ( Ju et al., 2023 ) , which contains 700 images spanning 10 edit types and provides a human-annotated editing mask for each example, together with source and target prompts. We report four metrics grouped into two aspects: (i) background preservation, measured outside the editing mask using LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) ; (ii) prompt–image consistency, measured by CLIP Similarity ( Radford et al., 2021 ) on the masked region, PickScore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) , and ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) . In extended results in Appendix E , we also report PSNR as another background metric, and a CLIP Similarity on the whole image. Full implementation details are deferred to Appendix F .

sections.heading: 5.1 The Impact of Vector-Field Smoothness
sections.text: We first study image reconstruction to isolate inversion error in EES schemes, and show that, as indicated in Section 3.1 , swapping to a model version fine-tuned to produce smoother trajectories (Smooth Diffusion; Guo et al. 2024 ) substantially improves EES reversibility, which translates to better background preservation in image editing.

sections.heading: 5.1.1 Image reconstruction
sections.text: In image reconstruction, given an image–caption pair, we invert the image to obtain a latent x T x_{T} and then reconstruct by running the solver back to x 0 x_{0} with the same caption. We report pixel-space mean squared error (MSE) computed on pixels normalised to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] , averaged over 100 images from the MS COCO 2014 ( Lin et al., 2014 ) Validation set. To match the image-editing setup, we fix a budget of 48 model evaluations per sample for all solvers. Supporting Wallace et al. (2023, Section D) , which observes that classifier-free guidance can induce vector-field roughness, Figure 2 shows that the EES schemes incur increasing reconstruction error as guidance grows, whereas the exactly reversible solvers remain largely unaffected. Repeating the experiment with the Smooth Diffusion ( Guo et al., 2024 ) fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 1.5 checkpoint substantially reduces this guidance sensitivity, suggesting that sufficiently smooth trajectories lead to reliable EES inversion. Figure 2 : Reconstruction MSE of (near) reversible solvers over 100 MS COCO 2014 images. EES schemes degrade with increasing guidance, but Smooth Diffusion greatly reduces this effect. The error bars represent 95% confidence intervals.

sections.heading: 5.1.2 Image editing
sections.text: We now show that the importance of trajectory smoothness for EES inversion observed in Section 5.1.1 translates to image editing quality. In Figure 3 , we compare EES under Stable Diffusion 1.5 and its Smooth Diffusion ( Guo et al., 2024 ) fine-tuned checkpoint. Using Smooth Diffusion largely preserves the background while still applying the intended edit. For quantitative evidence, we report full PIE-Bench results for both checkpoints across all solvers in Table 3 , and we also evaluate alternative smoothing heuristics that do not require changing the model, namely NPI and Proximal Guidance. Part 1 of Figure 7 visualises how Smooth Diffusion shifts each solver’s editing metrics. Since Smooth Diffusion does not benefit every solver equally, in subsequent sections we report, for each solver, the best-performing variant. Figure 3 : Qualitative editing comparison for EES under Stable Diffusion 1.5 (top) and Smooth Diffusion (bottom). Smooth Diffusion improves background preservation (e.g., the fence) while maintaining the intended edit. See Figure 15 for an extended grid including all solvers.

sections.heading: 5.3 Large Edits and Stability
sections.text: Here we highlight the main advantage of EES schemes over other reversible solvers: stability. We evaluate all solvers in regimes that induce large deviations from the original trajectory, and find that most exactly reversible solvers proposed in recent literature degrade substantially in edit quality, whereas EES remains stable and achieves the strongest performance across all metrics. We construct a large-prompt-deviations experiment from the random images category of PIE-Bench (140 images). For each image, we shift the target prompt by one position in the dataset, so the edit prompt is typically unrelated to the source image and may require a large semantic change. Since the original edit masks are no longer meaningful, we evaluate prompt alignment using CLIP similarity on the full image as our main metric, alongside PickScore and ImageReward. Here, we report all results using the Smooth Diffusion checkpoint. The Large Edits section of Table 2 shows that EES attains the strongest performance across metrics among the (near) reversible solvers under these large prompt deviations. Many exactly reversible solvers produce implausible outputs in this setting, failing to satisfy the new prompt condition when the required trajectory change is large. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion and Limitations
sections.text: We study reversible diffusion ODE solvers for inversion-based editing through the lens of editing stability, and show that exact reversibility alone is not enough: when an edit induces a large deviation from the inversion trajectory, existing reversible schemes can become numerically unstable and suffer sharp drops in quality. We address this with near-reversible EES solvers, which trade exact reversibility for substantially improved numerical stability. Empirically, EES is competitive with exactly reversible solvers on standard PIE-Bench edits and is the best-performing (near) reversible family in our study under large edits. While solver design is a crucial building block, making (near) reversible solvers production-quality image editors will require integrating them into more powerful pipelines. We aim to move reversible solvers closer to this goal by connecting them with existing image editing work: incorporating smoothing tricks, exploring ODE parametrisations, and benchmarking on PIE-Bench. Many directions remain open for future work, such as combining EES with attention-preservation methods like Prompt-to-Prompt ( Hertz et al., 2022 ) or MasaCtrl ( Cao et al., 2023 ) and extending evaluation beyond inversion-based methods (e.g., Zhang et al. (2023) ; Lugmayr et al. (2022) ; Tumanyan et al. (2023) ).

sections.text: This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.

sections.heading: Appendix E Additional Experiments
sections.text: Beyond the experiments in the main paper, in Section E.1 we report the full results of our image editing experiments, with and without Smooth Diffusion, and with three additional vector-field smoothing variants. In Section E.2 , we report the results of a large ablation over the ODE parametrisation, the step discretisation schedule, and whether the solver is applied in a semilinear integrating-factor form or a black-box form. This ablation justifies the solver forms proposed in Section 3 and highlights alternative forms that may also be used. We provide additional results for greyscale image editing in Section E.3 , experiments using SDXL in Section E.4 , results across different numbers of function evaluations in Section E.5 , and alternative EDICT and BDIA hyperparameter settings in Section E.6 . We also characterise the distribution of the inverted variable in Section E.7 and study the effect of varying the guidance scale in Section E.8 .

sections.heading: E.1 Smoothing Method Ablation
sections.text: Here, we study the impact of vector-field smoothing methods previously proposed to improve DDIM inversion and DDIM-based editing, and evaluate them on reversible and near-reversible solvers. To our knowledge, this has not been previously reported. We hope this study helps position reversible solvers within the broader DDIM inversion literature, where smoothing methods are widely used but typically treated as orthogonal to solver design. It is well known that DDIM inversion error typically increases with the classifier-free guidance scale, and several works propose inference-time tricks to mitigate this effect. Unlike Smooth Diffusion, these approaches do not modify model parameters. Instead, they change how conditioning is applied during inversion and/or sampling.

sections.heading: Vector-field smoothing and guidance tricks.
sections.text: Negative Prompt Inversion (NPI) ( Miyake et al., 2025 ) sets c null := c src c_{\texttt{null}}:=c_{\texttt{src}} , so the reverse-direction guidance cancels and the inversion becomes guidance-free: ϵ ^ θ ​ ( x t , t , c src ) = ϵ θ ​ ( x t , t , c src ) . \hat{\epsilon}_{\theta}(x_{t},t,c_{\texttt{src}})=\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{t},t,c_{\texttt{src}}). Proximal Guidance (Prox) ( Han et al., 2023 ) further reduces guidance in the forward (editing) direction by setting the guidance scale to g = 1 g=1 at spatial locations where the conditional predictions for the source and target prompts are already similar, that is, where ‖ ϵ ^ θ ​ ( x t , t , c trg ) − ϵ ^ θ ​ ( x t , t , c src ) ‖ 2 \left\lVert\hat{\epsilon}_{\theta}(x_{t},t,c_{\texttt{trg}})-\hat{\epsilon}_{\theta}(x_{t},t,c_{\texttt{src}})\right\rVert_{2} is small. Intuitively, Prox suppresses unnecessary conditional forcing in regions that are unlikely to change, which can reduce background drift. Both NPI and Prox were originally introduced in the context of DDIM-based editing. Here, we apply them across all solvers. Smooth Diffusion ( Guo et al., 2024 ) fine-tunes Stable Diffusion to produce smoother trajectories and reports improved DDIM inversion and editing. Since it changes the underlying model dynamics, it is complementary to NPI and Prox. Throughout this appendix, we use “smoothing method” as an umbrella term for both model-based smoothing (Smooth Diffusion) and inference-time guidance tricks (such as NPI and Proximal Guidance) that are designed to reduce inversion error and background drift.

sections.text: The above ODE-form does not prevent us from supporting discrete-time diffusion models, for which the noise schedule is defined at a discrete set of times α 0 , α 1 ​ … , α T \alpha_{0},\alpha_{1}\ldots,\alpha_{T} . Following the implementation in DPM ( Lu et al., 2022 ) , we construct a continuous α t \alpha_{t} by linearly interpolating log ⁡ α t \log\alpha_{t} between neighbouring discrete timesteps. We then set σ t = 1 − α t 2 \sigma_{t}=\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}^{2}} . While ( 25 ) is convenient conceptually, it requires approximating the gradient d ⁡ ( log ⁡ α t ) / d ​ t d(\log\alpha_{t})/dt , as part of the vector field. We therefore consider the following equivalent reparametrisations.

sections.text: Define the variable λ t \lambda_{t} as λ t := log ⁡ α t σ t = log ⁡ α t − log ⁡ σ t , \lambda_{t}:=\log\frac{\alpha_{t}}{\sigma_{t}}=\log\alpha_{t}-\log\sigma_{t}, which is strictly decreasing in t t and hence invertible. For VP schedules one can show d ​ log ⁡ α λ d ​ λ = σ λ 2 \frac{d\log\alpha_{\lambda}}{d\lambda}=\sigma_{\lambda}^{2} , and by change-of-variables the ODE becomes d ​ x λ d ​ λ = σ λ 2 ​ x λ − σ λ ​ ϵ θ ​ ( x λ , λ ) . \frac{dx_{\lambda}}{d\lambda}=\sigma_{\lambda}^{2}\,x_{\lambda}-\sigma_{\lambda}\,\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{\lambda},\lambda). sections.text: One can also define the integration variable u t := σ t α t = e − λ t , z t := x t α t . u_{t}:=\frac{\sigma_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}=e^{-\lambda_{t}},\qquad z_{t}:=\frac{x_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}. (28) Notably, this parametrisation removes the linear drift term entirely, so it can be treated as a purely non-linear ODE.

sections.heading: E.2.2 Semilinear vs. black-box
sections.text: A semilinear ODE in a variable λ \lambda has the form d ​ x λ d ​ λ = a λ ​ x λ + b ⁡ ( x λ , λ ) , \frac{dx_{\lambda}}{d\lambda}=a_{\lambda}x_{\lambda}+b(x_{\lambda},\lambda), where b b is non-linear (and in our setting contains a neural network). Black-box solvers (e.g. standard Runge–Kutta) discretise the full right-hand side, introducing discretisation error in both the linear and non-linear terms. In contrast, one can also solve such ODE using the integrating factor method, which solves the linear part exactly and leaves only a weighted integral of the non-linear part.

sections.heading: The integrating factor method.
sections.text: Define I λ = exp ( − ∫ λ a u d u ) , y λ = I λ x λ . I_{\lambda}=\exp\!\Bigl(-\int^{\lambda}a_{u}\,du\Bigr),\qquad y_{\lambda}=I_{\lambda}x_{\lambda}. Then y λ y_{\lambda} satisfies d ​ y λ d ​ λ = I λ ​ b ​ ( y λ I λ , λ ) , x λ = y λ I λ . \frac{dy_{\lambda}}{d\lambda}=I_{\lambda}\,b\!\Bigl(\frac{y_{\lambda}}{I_{\lambda}},\lambda\Bigr),\qquad x_{\lambda}=\frac{y_{\lambda}}{I_{\lambda}}. Since equations Equation 26 and Equation 27 are semilinear and the integrating factors simplify to 1 α λ \frac{1}{\alpha_{\lambda}} and 1 σ λ \frac{1}{\sigma_{\lambda}} , this method is of great convenience. We now present the solutions of the respective equations using the integrating factor method.

sections.heading: “Semilinear” solvers.
sections.text: When we report the metrics for a semilinear solver in Section E.2.4 , we apply the numerical method to the transformed ODE in y y (i.e. ( 29 ), ( 31 )) and then map back to x x . When we report a black-box solver, we apply the same numerical method directly to the original ODE in x x (i.e. ( 26 ), ( 27 )). Finally, the scaled-noise parametrisation ( 28 ) has no linear drift term, so it does not require an integrating factor.

sections.heading: E.2.3 Step discretisation schedule
sections.text: For each ODE parametrisation, we consider two choices of step schedule.

sections.heading: Uniform steps in the integration variable.
sections.text: Given an integration variable τ \tau (such as λ , u \lambda,u ), we take τ \tau -uniform steps by linearly spacing the grid { τ 0 , … , τ N } \{\tau_{0},\dots,\tau_{N}\} between the endpoints and applying the solver with constant step size Δ ​ τ = ( τ N − τ 0 ) / N \Delta\tau=(\tau_{N}-\tau_{0})/N .

sections.heading: Steps induced by a uniform t t -grid.
sections.text: Alternatively, we start from a uniform grid in the original diffusion time t t , i.e. t i = i / N t_{i}=i/N , and map it to the integration variable τ \tau via τ i := τ ⁡ ( t i ) \tau_{i}:=\tau(t_{i}) . This yields a non-uniform step size Δ ​ τ i = τ i + 1 − τ i \Delta\tau_{i}=\tau_{i+1}-\tau_{i} .

sections.heading: E.2.4 Results
sections.text: To evaluate a given ODE configuration, we run the 140 editing tasks in the random images category of PIE-Bench and report CLIP and LPIPS. Figure 8 shows a systematic evaluation over the three design dimensions introduced above and motivates the configurations used in Section 3 . For the EES schemes, edit fidelity is already strong across settings, so we select the variant that most consistently improves background preservation. This corresponds to the semilinear formulation with λ \lambda -uniform discretisation and the half-logSNR x x -parameterisation for both EES(2,5) and EES(2,7). Across solvers, λ \lambda -uniform discretisation tends to yield better reversibility than t t -uniform discretisation, while the remaining design dimensions have a smaller effect. For Reversible Heun, which is already strong in reversibility relative to other solvers, we choose the configuration with the best overall balance of edit alignment and background preservation. This is the black-box formulation with t t -uniform discretisation and the half-logSNR x x -parameterisation. The difference between half-logSNR x x - and ϵ \epsilon -parameterisations is minor in this setting. We also observe that, for Reversible Heun, the black-box formulation generally outperforms the semilinear one. We use the same choices for our implementation of McCallum-Foster (Euler) and McCallum-Foster (Midpoint). We have observed slow convergence for the semilinear formulation when using the half-logSNR in x x parametrisation with a t t -uniform discretisation, and the scaled-noise parametrisation with a u u -uniform discretisation. They do not produce satisfactory images in our setting of 48 48 model evaluations. We therefore omit these combinations from further study. Figure 8 : Ablations over solver configuration on the random images category of PIE-Bench. Each panel plots edit prompt alignment against background preservation for EES(2,5), EES(2,7), and Reversible Heun. We vary three separate dimensions: ODE parametrisation (marker shape: original ( 25 ), half logSNR in ϵ \epsilon ( 26 ) and x x ( 27 ), sigma ( 28 )), discretisation variable (text label t / λ t/\lambda indicates uniform steps in that variable), and formulation (colour indicates semilinear vs black-box). We report this using Smooth Diffusion for EES and Stable Diffusion 1.5 for Reversible Heun, since Section E.1 shows that smoothing methods do not improve Reversible Heun.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2605.16399v1 [cs.CV] 12 May 2026 Stable and Near-Reversible Diffusion ODE Solvers for Image Editing Barbora Barancikova Affiliation: Department of Computing, Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom Correspondence to: b.barancikova23@imperial.ac.uk Daniil Shmelev Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom Cristopher Salvi Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom Abstract The inversion of diffusion models plays a central role in image editing. Algebraically reversible ODE solvers provide an appealing approach to diffusion inversion for text-guided image editing, by eliminating the inversion error inherent in DDIM-based editing pipelines. However, empirical results indicate that reversibility alone is insufficient. As edits require larger semantic or visual changes, reversible diffusion solvers often exhibit instabilities and suffer sharp drops in output quality. In this paper, we show that the trade-off between exact reversibility and numerical stability manifests empirically as a trade-off between background preservation and prompt alignment in image editing. We then investigate the use of near-reversible Runge–Kutta methods as a more stable alternative to exactly reversible diffusion schemes. When combined with a vector-field smoothing strategy, the resulting approach improves edit fidelity, remains stable under large edits, and largely retains the background-preservation benefits of reversible solvers. Keywords: Machine Learning, ICML 1 Introduction Diffusion probabilistic models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2020b ) have become a standard tool for text-guided image editing ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Nichol et al., 2021 ) . A common approach is inversion-based editing —given a real image, the probability-flow ODE ( Song et al., 2020b ) is integrated backwards in time to a latent noise state conditional on a source prompt, after which the forward ODE is integrated under a new target prompt to obtain an edited image ( Song et al., 2020a ; Mokady et al., 2023 ; Ju et al., 2023 ) . (a) Small Edits (b) Large Edits Figure 1 : Qualitative comparison of (near) reversible solvers on image editing tasks. ( 1(a) ) Standard PIE-Bench editing tasks ( Section 5.2 ). Here, we use Smooth Diffusion for BELM, EDICT, and EES. ( 1(b) ) PIE-Bench images with large prompt deviations ( Section 5.3 ) and greyscale conversion ( Section E.3 ). Here, we use Smooth Diffusion for all methods. See extended grids in Figures 17 , 15 , 18 and 9 . In this setting, the choice of numerical solver is vital, since errors resulting from inexact inversion compound through the editing process, especially under classifier-free guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ) . For instance, classical DDIM inversion incurs a systematic trajectory mismatch, since the reverse update is not the algebraic inverse of the forward update. A long line of work aims to reduce the resulting diffusion inversion error ( Han et al., 2023 ; Miyake et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2024 ) . Recently, algebraically reversible (or simply reversible ) ODE solvers such as EDICT ( Wallace et al., 2023 ) , BDIA ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , BELM ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , and Rex ( Blasingame and Liu, 2026 ) have been proposed as an alternative to DDIM inversion, yielding improved reconstructions and background preservation in editing pipelines. However, our empirical evidence suggests that reversibility alone is not enough. On standard editing tasks, reversible solvers exhibit a clear trade-off between background preservation and prompt alignment. This becomes particularly apparent when the editing trajectory departs substantially from the inversion trajectory, in which case many reversible solvers suffer sharp drops in edit quality. To benchmark solver performance for image editing, we distinguish two evaluation settings. The first is the widely used small edits setting of the PIE-Bench image editing benchmark introduced by Ju et al. (2023) , where edits are usually local to a subset of the prompt and image (see Section 5.2 ). In addition, we introduce a second large edits regime, where the edited prompt induces a large semantic or visual change, forcing the sampling trajectory away from the original inversion path (see Section 5.3 ). Figure 1 previews the key findings. In Section 4 , we argue that the failure modes of existing reversible schemes, illustrated in Figure 1 , can be attributed to numerical stability. To address these issues, we propose using the recently introduced class of near-reversible Explicit and Effectively Symmetric (EES) Runge–Kutta methods ( Shmelev et al., 2025 ) as diffusion solvers. EES schemes relax exact reversibility, instead enforcing only approximate symmetry up to an acceptably low error tolerance. This relaxation allows them to retain an explicit Runge–Kutta form and benefit from much more favourable stability properties. Since the inversion error depends on the regularity of the underlying trajectory, we additionally combine EES schemes with vector-field smoothing strategies previously proposed for DDIM inversion. Together, this yields a family of solvers that is competitive with exactly reversible solvers on standard editing benchmarks and substantially more stable under challenging edits. In addition to proposing EES solvers, our paper clarifies the broader design space of reversible diffusion solvers for editing. We investigate guidance and smoothing heuristics such as Smooth Diffusion ( Guo et al., 2024 ) , Negative Prompt Inversion ( Miyake et al., 2025 ) , and Proximal Guidance ( Han et al., 2023 ) , which have previously been treated mainly as orthogonal DDIM-based techniques. We show that these methods can also yield substantial gains for reversible solvers, and characterise when they help. We also benchmark Reversible Heun and McCallum–Foster methods, originally introduced outside the diffusion models literature, and run extensive ablations over ODE parametrisations, step schedules, and solver formulations. We summarise our main contributions as follows: 1. We provide a side-by-side evaluation of (near) reversible diffusion solvers for image editing, revealing a trade-off curve between background preservation and prompt alignment. 2. We propose using near-reversible EES Runge–Kutta methods for inversion-based diffusion editing. For small edits , when combined with vector field smoothing, these methods retain much of the background-preservation benefit of exactly reversible solvers while improving edit fidelity. 3. For large edits , we show that EES is the most robust (near) reversible family in our study, maintaining output quality under large trajectory deviations where most exactly reversible solvers degrade substantially. 2 Preliminaries 2.1 Reversible Solvers In the setting of an autonomous ODE d ​ y t = f ⁡ ( y t ) ​ d ​ t dy_{t}=f(y_{t})dt , a one-step method y n + 1 = y n + h ​ Φ h ​ ( y n ) y_{n+1}=y_{n}+h\Phi_{h}(y_{n}) (1) is said to be symmetric if Φ − h = Φ h − 1 \Phi_{-h}=\Phi_{h}^{-1} . That is, a step of the method Φ \Phi applied to y n + 1 y_{n+1} with a negative step size exactly recovers y n y_{n} . Classical symmetric numerical integration methods, such as those of Runge–Kutta type, have been studied extensively for their favourable long-term behaviour, especially in the context of Hamiltonian systems ( Hairer et al., 2006 ; Feng and Qin, 2010 ; Chartier, 2015 ) . More recently, symmetric methods have proven useful in the training of neural differential equations ( Chen et al., 2018 ) , where the ability to recover the full solution trajectory from the terminal point allows for memory-efficient backpropagation. A major drawback of classical symmetric methods lies in their low efficiency. It is well-known that any symmetric Runge–Kutta scheme is necessarily implicit, and more generally any symmetric parasitism-free general linear method cannot be explicit ( Butcher et al., 2016 ) . This inefficiency makes classical schemes unsuitable for applications in machine learning. To solve this problem, several new algebraically reversible schemes, typically of low-order, were introduced. The asynchronous leapfrog integrator (ALF) ( Zhuang et al., 2021 ) for Neural ODEs overcomes the problem of implicit schemes by tracking an auxiliary state as part of the integration. A similar approach is taken by the Reversible Heun method ( Kidger et al., 2021 ) , where the technique of tracking an auxiliary state is applied to form a reversible version of Heun’s method for SDEs. Whilst both methods prove to be efficient, they are inherently unstable. This instability is a significant bottleneck in certain practical applications ( Shmelev and Salvi, 2025 ; Zhang and Chen, 2021 ) . In ( McCallum and Foster, 2024 ) , a new method was proposed for transforming any existing one-step integration method into one which is reversible. Whilst these methods offer increased stability over the ALF and Reversible Heun solvers, their stability domains are still typically much smaller than those of classical methods. This method was later adapted to the case of diffusion models, where the approach forms the basis for Rex solvers ( Blasingame and Liu, 2026 ) . A potential solution to the issues of stability is offered by Explicit and Effectively Symmetric (EES) Runge–Kutta schemes ( Shmelev et al., 2025 ) . A concrete example of this reduced stability is given by the second Dahlquist barrier ( Dahlquist, 1963 ) , which famously states that no multi-step method of order greater than 2 can be A-stable. The stability of multi-step methods can be difficult to analyse, especially in the case of time-varying coefficients such as the ones used by the BELM sampler ( 9 ). A common proxy for the stability of a linear method is zero-stability , which requires that small perturbations to the initial condition lead to small changes in the numerical solution. An equivalent definition which is aligned closer with the notion of linear-stability of one-step methods is given by the following. Definition 4.1 (Zero-Stability) . Given a linear multistep method, let P P denote the characteristic polynomial which arises from the application of the method to the equation y ′ = 0 y^{\prime}=0 . The method is said to be zero-stable if all roots ζ \zeta of P P satisfy the root condition | ζ | ≤ 1 |\zeta|\leq 1 . As discussed in Wang et al. (2024) , both DDIM and BELM are zero-stable, whilst the zero-stability of the EDICT and BDIA solvers is unclear. Whilst zero-stability is a useful metric for multi-step solvers, the condition is significantly weaker than that of the linear stability of one-step methods. As we will see, the stability guarantees of EES schemes far exceed those of zero-stability. 4.2 One-Step Methods We begin by defining the more general notion of linear stability . Definition 4.2 . We construct a large-prompt-deviations experiment from the random images category of PIE-Bench (140 images).
